distinguishing_features: Active impressed-current cathodic polarization of the titanium anode to move its surface potential below a corrosion threshold into an immunity region.
Use of an inert counter-electrode/anode bed and reversible DC rectifier to deliver protective current in the anolyte.
Closed-loop control using a local reference-electrode potential threshold rather than scheduled chemical dosing.
Protection of the titanium coating substrate by lowering operating potential instead of raising pitting resistance with an inhibitor film.
parsed.objective_technical_problem: How to reduce potential-driven electrochemical dissolution of a titanium anode coating/substrate in chloride-bearing chlor-alkali anolyte during cell operation.
parsed.viable_reason: The candidate is not viable as written because cathodically polarizing an operating chlor-alkali anode conflicts with its required anodic function, the -5 mA/cm² and -100 mV vs Ag/AgCl setpoints do not reach Ti immunity, and existing cell-voltage sensors do not provide the local reference potential needed for the control loop.
parsed.non_obvious_reason: Impressed-current cathodic protection and reference-electrode potential control are conventional corrosion-control measures, so once the problem is cast as potential-driven dissolution, substituting them for inhibitor-based E_pit elevation would be an obvious step to a skilled engineer.
